Beyond the visible lesion: mycotoxin attenuation and spatial heterogeneity in maize cobs
nodes.venue: Mycotoxin Research
nodes.abstract: Abstract Visible mould is widely used as a practical sorting cue in maize, but it remains unclear whether the visible lesion marks the boundary of mycotoxin contamination within an intact cob. This study examined mycotoxin attenuation, spatial heterogeneity, and co-occurrence in visibly mouldy white maize cobs, using measured distances from the visible mould margin. Cobs with visible mould ( n = 35) were sampled for the study. For each cob, the visible mould margin was coded as 0 mm, and adjacent sections were collected at the 50% and 75% points along the measured distance from the lesion boundary to the distal cob tip, resulting in 98 cob-section observations. Mycotoxins, FUMs (FB1, FB2, FB3), deoxynivalenol (DON), zearalenone (ZEA), nivalenol (NIV) and AF (AFB1) were quantified by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Samples with no detectable levels of mycotoxins were replaced with zero, and total FUMs were calculated (FB1 + FB2 + FB3). The visible mould margin accounted for the largest share of the measured toxin burden, accounting for 84.4% of total FUM, 89.4% of DON, 77.8% of ZEA, and 92.2% of NIV. Adjacent sections retained measurable residual mycotoxins, including 15.6% of total FUM, 10.6% of DON, 22.2% of ZEA, and 7.8% of NIV. In full-distance models, DON, ZEA, and NIV declined significantly with distance, whereas total FUM did not show significant monotonic attenuation. The AFB1 was detected in only three cob sections; these detections co-occurred with Fusarium -associated toxins. Co-occurrence analysis showed that adjacent sections frequently remained positive for multiple Fusarium -associated toxin groups, with the FUM + DON + ZEA profile persisting across measured-distance bands. These findings show that visible mould is a useful warning signal but not a reliable toxicological boundary. The results support cob-level rejection or segregation of visibly mouldy cobs before shelling, rather than lesion-level trimming, as a more defensible food-safety control measure.

nodes.name: Research on the Dynamic and Communication Mode of Public Opinion Emotions Based on Text Mining and Sentiment Analysis
nodes.venue: 電腦學刊
nodes.abstract: The swift dissemination of public opinions on university-related events is inevitably associated with topic variations, emotions, and complicated interpersonal interaction among the users. To explore this problem, this study proposes a hybrid framework including text mining, sentiment analysis, and opinion evolution modeling based on fuzzy theory. Data about public opinions will be collected on social platforms like Weibo, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu, then will be subjected to data cleaning, Chinese word segmentation, and stop-word elimination. An optimized version of BERTopic is employed to detect topics by means of domain knowledge mapping, keyword pre-exploration, topic labeling via assistance of large language models and fine-tuning of embedding models. Sentiment tendencies will be further divided into types with help of a model that combines RoBERTa-BiLSTM and interactive attention and biaffine feature fusion. Based on these analyses, a fuzzy opinion-evolution model is built to evaluate the impact of peer trust, opinion leader trust, timely and credible responses on emotions and consensus. A case of university cafeteria-related public opinion event will be adopted for empirical analysis. The findings indicate that the proposed framework can identify theme and emotion variations in campus public opinion. Higher opinion leader trust can speed up inter-group consensus while too much reliance on peer interactions may delay it. Late and low credibility responses are likely to increase public opinion risk.

nodes.name: Leveraging Mamba for Enhanced Multimodal Few-Shot Action Recognition
nodes.venue: 電腦學刊
nodes.abstract: Few-Shot Action Recognition (FSAR) widely use in Action Recognition domains with limited labeled data, such as medical surgery. Existing FSAR methods often rely on single-modal approaches, which suffer from limited feature representation and a lack of semantic understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoMA, a novel Mamba-based multimodal FSAR framework, designed to optimize the learning of multimodal information and improve the performance of few-shot action recognition tasks. MoMA integrates a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to generate semantically rich representations from both textual and video data, which are then aligned and fused with visual features. To address the challenges of domain-specific prior knowledge and intra-class variance, we introduce a dual-branch contrastive learning architecture that reinforces category distinctions and mitigates the accumulation of intra-class heterogeneity. Our experimental results show that MoMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the HMDB51, Kinetics, and SSv2 datasets, achieving improvements of 1.5%, 1.9%, and 3.5%, respectively, in the 1-shot setting.

nodes.name: <b>Random Forest-Based Vegetation and Non-Vegetation Classification in Siak Regency Using Landsat 8 and Google Earth Engine</b>
nodes.venue: Jurnal Teknoif Teknik Informatika Institut Teknologi Padang
nodes.abstract: Monitoring vegetation degradation is essential for supporting sustainable land resource management through accurate and continuous land cover assessment. This quantitative study classifies vegetation in Siak Regency, Riau Province, using Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance (Level-2) imagery from 2024 and the Random Forest (RF) algorithm in the Google Earth Engine (GEE) environment. Fifty purposively selected ground truth samples, categorized as vegetation and non-vegetation, were used. Spectral bands were combined with three vegetation indices, namely NDVI, SAVI, and EVI, to improve classification performance. The dataset was randomly split into 70% training data (33 samples) and 30% validation data (17 samples) to maintain reproducibility. The model achieved an Overall Accuracy of 88.24% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.757, indicating substantial agreement between predicted and reference classes. The integration of the three indices provided complementary spectral information, improving the model’s ability to distinguish vegetation density, atmospheric influence, and soil background sensitivity. However, the small validation dataset and binary classification scheme limit the statistical reliability of the results and their comparability with multi-class studies. Overall, the findings show that combining Random Forest and Google Earth Engine offers an efficient and scalable approach to vegetation mapping. Future studies should use larger datasets, more robust validation strategies, and finer land cover classification schemes to improve reliability in tropical environmental monitoring.

Authentica AI: An Explainable Multimodal System for Synthetic Media Detection Using Deep Features, Reconstruction Error and Frequency-Domain Forensics
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: The rapid improvement of generative models has made AI-generated images, cloned voices and manipulated video increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic media, while most deployed detectors examine a single modality and return an opaque score. This paper presents Authentica AI, a web-based multimodal synthetic-media detection system that automatically routes each upload to a modality-specific detector. Images are analysed by a pretrained convolutional backbone (EfficientNetB0, with a ResNet-50 variant), a diffusion-reconstruction error map, and five handcrafted forensic signals — spectral energy loss, spatial variation, edge-sharpness consistency, colour-channel correlation and local-variance entropy — which are fused by a weighted ensemble and a calibrated sigmoid into a single synthetic-probability score. Audio is converted to log-Mel spectrograms and classified by a ResNet-18 model. Every image verdict is accompanied by a forensic heatmap that localises the regions that drove the decision, and results are stored in a PostgreSQL database and presented through an interactive dashboard with batch processing. In a prototype evaluation on a five-image batch the system returned verdicts with a mean latency of 263.3 ms per image on a CPU, and per-stage profiling of a single run (288.1 ms) shows that the reconstruction stages account for about two thirds of the processing time. The paper also states the limits of this evaluation: no labelled benchmark accuracy is reported, and large-scale benchmarking and video support are identified as future work.

nodes.name: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
Advanced Digital Image and Signal Processing Techniques for Real-Time Anomaly Detection
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: Real-time anomaly detection is a core requirement in industrial monitoring, surveillance, biomedical diagnostics and predictive maintenance, where unusual events must be identified within strict latency limits. This paper presents a unified framework that combines digital image processing (DIP) and digital signal processing (DSP) techniques for detecting anomalies in streaming visual and one-dimensional sensor data. The framework consists of modality-specific pre-processing, spatial and time–frequency feature extraction, feature-level fusion, unsupervised anomaly scoring and an adaptive decision threshold. Techniques reviewed and integrated include adaptive background modelling, optical flow, edge and texture analysis, the shorttime Fourier transform, wavelet decomposition, statistical indicators, autoencoder reconstruction error and isolation-based scoring. Real-time design considerations such as sliding-window processing, computational complexity and embedded deployment are discussed, and an evaluation protocol based on precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and detection latency is defined. The framework is demonstrated on reproducible synthetic vibration-signal and surface-image data; the signal pipeline achieved an F1-score of 0.949 with a per-window processing time of about 2.0 ms, and the image pipeline achieved a recall of 1.000 at about 1.6 ms per frame on a general-purpose processor. A qualitative comparison of methods and a set of design guidelines are provided to help practitioners select a suitable technique for a given application and hardware budget.

nodes.name: DeepGuard: A Robust Multimodal Framework for Automated Deepfake Screening and Triage
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: Deepfakes are synthetic images, videos, and voice recordings produced by deep generative models, and their realism now exceeds what human observers can reliably judge. Most existing detectors address a single medium, which leaves them blind to forgeries that live in motion or in sound. This paper presents DeepGuard, a unified multimodal framework that accepts an image, a video, or an audio file through one web interface and returns a Real or Deepfake verdict together with a confidence percentage. Uploaded media are normalized and, for video, separated into frames and an audio track. YOLOv8-Face localizes and crops the facial region, a ResNet-50 convolutional network extracts spatial forgery cues such as texture irregularities and blending artifacts, a bidirectional long short-term memory network models frame-to-frame inconsistencies, and a Wav2Vec2 model examines the speech signal for synthetic or cloned voices. A Bayesian weighted fusion stage combines whichever modality predictions are available into one deepfake probability, which is thresholded and stored with its metadata in a history database. The system is implemented with a Flask backend, OpenCV, and NumPy. The paper details the design rationale, the algorithm of each module, the fusion rule, and a leakage-free evaluation protocol based on accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and a confusion matrix. Quantitative results are intentionally not reported here; they will be added after experiments on benchmark datasets.

nodes.name: Development and Functional Testing of a Web Based Dengue Weather Alert Prototype with WhatsApp Notifications in Palu, Indonesia
nodes.venue: Healthy Tadulako Journal (Jurnal Kesehatan Tadulako)
nodes.abstract: Background: Weather information may support dengue preparedness, although software functionality alone cannot establish forecasting accuracy. Objectives: This study developed a web based weather alert prototype integrating meteorological data and WhatsApp notifications for dengue preparedness in Palu, Indonesia. Methods: Research and development followed the Analysis, Design, and Development phases of the ADDIE model from January 14 to February 4, 2026. CodeIgniter 4 and MySQL supported coordinate based weather retrieval through OpenWeather, data storage, user registration, and automated notifications. Results: The prototype covered 46 urban villages across eight districts. Nine functional testing categories were reported as successful, including website accessibility, geographic data, weather integration, storage, notifications, decision logic, registration, profile management, and interface responsiveness. However, detailed test inputs, execution counts, and notification delivery receipts were unavailable. The 22 day development period could not independently establish a complete 30 day rainfall dataset without historical records. Weather thresholds remained literature informed assumptions without local predictive validation. Conclusions: The prototype demonstrated preliminary software integration capabilities. Reproducible functional testing, rainfall data verification, governance safeguards, and independent epidemiological validation are required before operational implementation for dengue preparedness.

nodes.name: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Detection of AI-Generated Images
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has enabled the production of highly realistic synthetic images that are increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic visual content. Although deep learning-based detection methods have demonstrated promising performance in identifying AI-generated images, many existing approaches operate as black-box models and provide limited explanations for their predictions. This lack of interpretability creates challenges for applications where users need to understand why an image has been classified as authentic or synthetic. This paper proposes an Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Detection of AI-Generated Images that combines deep visual feature learning with explainable artificial intelligence techniques. The proposed framework analyzes spatial and potentially frequency-domain characteristics of images, extracts discriminative features using a convolutional or transformer-based deep learning architecture, and classifies images into real and AI-generated categories. An explainability layer is incorporated using techniques such as Grad-CAM, saliency analysis, or related post-hoc explanation methods to identify image regions contributing to the model's decision. The framework is designed to evaluate not only classification performance but also robustness, generalization to unseen image-generation models, and interpretability. Existing literature indicates that cross-generator generalization remains a significant challenge because detector performance can decline when images originate from generators or scenes not represented during training. The proposed framework therefore emphasizes generalized detection and visual explanation rather than accuracy alone. The study is expected to contribute a transparent and reproducible approach for AIgenerated image forensics and provide a foundation for trustworthy synthetic-media detection.

nodes.name: A PRIVACY PRESERVING PERSONAL AI ASSISTANT AND THE COST OF CLOUD MODEL INFERENCE: ARCHITECTURE, CAPABILITY TRADEOFFS, AND EVALUATION PROTOCOL
nodes.venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
nodes.abstract: Personal AI assistants need reliable research and controlled access to private data. This report specifies a local-first Windows architecture and examines the capability, privacy, and operating-cost tradeoff between local Llama 3.2 3B through Ollama and self-hosted Kimi K2.5 on rented NVIDIA GPUs. We analyzed a supplied project design summary, mapped trust boundaries and failure modes, and calculated illustrative costs from a documented eight-H200 deployment and published rental rates. The design separates public research from authenticated browser sessions, enforces permissions outside the model, and requires evidence-supported answers. At an illustrative $4.59 per GPU-hour, eight H200s cost $36.72 per running hour, $4,406.40 for four hours daily over 30 days, or $26,438.40 for continuous 30-day operation, before storage and operations. An assumed 100 W incremental local draw for four hours daily at $0.15/kWh costs $1.80 monthly on an existing PC. These are scenarios, not measured deployments. Kimi K2.5 offers multimodal and agentic capabilities that a text-only 3B baseline should not be assumed to match; no matched end-to-end test was performed. Stronger cloud inference can impose substantial dedicated GPU rental cost and transfers prompts to a cloud operator. Local inference preserves a narrower data boundary at far lower incremental cash cost but requires direct task-quality evaluation.

Adaptive Machine Learning in Non-Stationary Environments: A Systematic Review of Concept Drift Detection and Mitigation in Data Streams
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: The proliferation of high-velocity data streams in domains such as IoT, cybersecurity, and financial technology has exposed the limitations of static machine learning models. When the underlying data distribution changes over time, a phenomenon known as concept drift occurs, leading to severe model degradation `[1]`. This paper presents a systematic review of 29 foundational and contemporary studies on concept drift detection and adaptation. We categorize detection mechanisms into statistical, window-based, and model-based approaches, while evaluating adaptation strategies ranging from dynamic ensembles to lightweight incremental learning `[16]`. Furthermore, we address compounding challenges, including class imbalance and the emergence of novel classes `[2]`, `[30]`. By synthesizing recent advancements, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing robust, real-time, and resource-efficient streaming machine learning systems `[27]`

nodes.name: Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Underwater Species Detection and Classification
nodes.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
nodes.abstract: Underwater fish detection is challenging. Fish can be very small in images. The contrast in scenes is often weak. Turbid water can hide details. When fish overlap it becomes harder to locate each one. This study compares deeplearning object detectors using an underwater fish dataset. The focus is on both detection quality and how well the models work in video processing. The models tested are YOLO26, RF-DETR and SSD300 with a backbone. In the evaluations YOLO26s achieved a mAP@50 of 0.875 and a mAP@50:95 of 0.499. RF-DETR Base reached 0.4465 and 0.3085 respectively. The SSD300 model showed a precision of 0.8611, recall of 0.1975, mAP@50 of 0.1436 and mAP@50:95 of 0.0607. These results show that high precision alone does not mean detection performance if recall is low. The comparison also looks at class-label consistency and differences, in settings. The model runs were not all done under the conditions. Still the results give a view of what each detector can do. They highlight the strengths and weaknesses of YOLO26, RF-DETR and SSD300 for detecting fish in underwater.

nodes.name: Breaking GUI Agent Actions: Realistic Adversarial Attacks on Multimodal LLMs
nodes.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
nodes.abstract: Recent progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has enabled GUI agents that interpret interface screenshots and execute natural-language instructions. However, their increasing role in human–computer interaction raises security concerns. Existing work shows that MLLMs are highly sensitive to interface perturbations, yet most attacks assume unrealistic capabilities such as direct access to model-ready inputs. In real deployments, attackers cannot control the screenshot pipeline or the non-differentiable preprocessing operations preceding inference, rendering many prior attacks ineffective. We introduce Realistic Adversarial Attack (RAA) framework that models the complete screenshot-to-prediction pipeline. To address gradient blockage from non-differentiable preprocessing (e.g., resizing and quantization), we develop a dual-branch differentiable preprocessing module that restores gradient flow while remaining faithful to the actual inference path. To improve robustness against query phrasing changes, we further incorporate a task-level semantic variation mechanism that jointly optimizes over paraphrased task variants. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B-Instruct and GUI-Owl-7B show that RAA consistently outperforms prior attacks, improving attack success rates by an average of 30% under localized perturbations and a 10.7% under global perturbations, while maintaining strong effectiveness against standard defenses such as resizing, compression, and noise. Ablation studies highlight the roles of perturbation region and semantic diversity. Our framework establishes a practical threat model for GUI agents and offers a foundation for future robustness and security research.

nodes.name: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
When Does Virtual Visitation Become Tourism? A Boundary Model of Remote Tourism Participation
nodes.venue: Tourism and Hospitality
nodes.abstract: Digital platforms enable encounters with museums, heritage sites, wildlife reserves, and destination replicas without corporeal travel, yet tourism scholarship lacks a defensible rule for deciding when such an episode constitutes tourism participation and not media consumption, education, or promotion. This conceptual theory article develops an episode-level boundary model of remote tourism participation through problematisation and integrative theoretical synthesis. Three constitutive tests are derived: destination orientation, mediated spatial encounter, and visitor-position enactment. All three must be evidenced, although their empirical manifestations may vary across technologies and cultural settings. Destination-linked consequences are treated as evaluative outcomes rather than inclusion requirements. The model is stress-tested against guided virtual museum visits, interactive wildlife livestreams, metaverse destination replicas, documentaries, promotional simulations, and booking searches. It distinguishes remote participation from tourism facilitation, destination media consumption, and non-touristic virtual activities whilst differentiating between autonomous, preparatory, and complementary episodes. The study extends stationary-tourism scholarship by treating non-movement as a scope condition rather than a sufficient definition and by shifting classification from technologies to realised participant–destination relations. The model offers researchers a proposed auditable classification procedure, provides managers with design and evaluation criteria, and enables policymakers to recognise remote participation without conflating it with physical arrivals.
